title: How to prevent leaks from Claude Code's 'Don't ask again' file
summary:
This guide details how to find and remove secrets that were inadvertently committed to projects and repositories hosted on GitLab. We’ve confirmed that GitLab’s own infrastructure secrets are protected.

In Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding agent, a developer can approve a shell command by selecting “Yes, and don’t ask again.” Claude then saves that exact command to .claude/settings.local.json in the project folder and runs it without asking in the future. If the command contained a password or a token, so does the file:

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(npm test:*)",
      "Bash(curl --header \"PRIVATE-TOKEN: glpat-EXAMPLEdummyTOKEN1234\" \"https://gitlab.com/api/v4/projects/1234567/issues?state=closed\")",
    ]
  }
}

Claude Code keeps the file out of Git through the developer's personal global excludes, not through the project's .gitignore. That protection lives on one laptop and does not travel with the repository, so the file gets committed and pushed wherever the repository lives. In early November 2026, Apiiro reported that this issue resulted in 104,185 copies of the file to appear in public repositories, 1,122 of them holding at least one secret. Hundreds more secrets were only in history, in files that had since been deleted.

If your developers use Claude Code with repositories hosted on GitLab, this guide shows how to prevent this from happening moving forward, assess exposure now or in the past, and clean every affected project up at once.

Prevent: Keep the file out of your repo

There are a few actions you can perform to ensure a developer cannot commit the file by accident, and that if one slips through, you hear about it. There are four layers you can put in place, each a little more work than the last, and the order below is a reasonable one to follow. All of them are settings a group owner changes once; this is the one part of the process GitLab Duo can walk you through but cannot do for you, since its access to GitLab settings is read-only.

Start with .gitignore

The simplest fix is also the one Claude Code should have done for you but does not: a line in each repository's .gitignore that reads .claude/settings.local.json. Claude Code only ever adds the exclusion to the developer's own global git configuration, which stays on that laptop.

If you're on Premium or Ultimate, put the same line into the .gitignore in your group's file templates project (in the group, go to Settings > General > Templates), so that every project created from now on inherits it without anyone having to remember.

Block the file name with a push rule (Premium and Ultimate)

A push rule turns the convention into something GitLab enforces. In the group, go to Settings > Repository > Pre-defined push rules and, under Prohibited filenames, enter:

(^|/)\.claude/settings\.local\.json$

From then on, any push that tries to add that file, in the root of the repository or in any subdirectory, on any branch, is rejected before it lands, and the developer sees a message naming the pattern.

There are two things to know about how push rules behave, both of which matter here. The rule only checks files being added, not changes to a file that is already tracked, which is why cleaning up the existing copies has to come first. And a rule set on the group is copied into projects created after that moment; it does not reach back to projects that already exist. For those, you set the same rule on each project, either from the project's own Settings > Repository > Push rules page or, if you have more than a handful, with a loop over the group's project ids:

POST /api/v4/projects//push_rule
{"file_name_regex": "(^|/)\\.claude/settings\\.local\\.json$"}

For a project that already has push rules of its own, use PUT on the same path instead; POST will answer 422 Project push rule exists.

Add Secret Push Protection for the tokens (Ultimate)

The push rule stops the file by name. Secret Push Protection looks at the content of every push, whatever the file is called, and rejects it if it finds a known token format. On GitLab Self-Managed and Dedicated, you first allow the feature for the instance under Admin > Settings > Security and compliance; on GitLab.com, that part is already done. Then you turn it on for each project under Secure > Security configuration > Secret push protection, or for a whole group at once through the group security settings API.

Scan everything with one policy (Ultimate)

A scan execution policy on the top-level group runs GitLab Secret Detection in every project, including ones that have no .gitlab-ci.yml at all, and individual projects can't switch it off. Create it under Group > Secure > Policies > New policy > Scan execution policy, with one rule that runs on every pipeline and a second that runs on a weekly schedule. The scheduled run looks through history the first time it runs; add the variable SECRET_DETECTION_HISTORIC_SCAN: 'true' to that rule if you want every weekly run to cover full history rather than only new commits. It detects the same token formats as push protection and also covers what is already in the repository, including history when the historic scan is on.

Assess: Do you have the file?

Once you’ve put the preventative measures in place, you want to know whether .claude/settings.local.json exists anywhere in your repositories, either now or at some point in the past. What the file contains only matters once you have the list of affected repositories, and there are a few ways to get it depending on what your GitLab subscription includes.

Ask GitLab Duo

If your group has GitLab Duo (Duo Core on Premium and Ultimate, or GitLab Credits on a Free group on GitLab.com), the quickest route is to open GitLab Duo Agentic Chat, part of the GitLab Duo Agent Platform, in your top-level group and paste this:

Has any project in the  group ever had a file named .claude/settings.local.json, including projects where the file was later deleted and projects where it only exists on a branch other than the default? For each project, tell me whether it has the file now, and if not, the commit where it was added and the commit where it was removed. Explain how you checked.

GitLab Duo works through the group and its subgroups, queries each project's commit history for that exact path, lists the branches of any project with a hit, and fetches the current file to distinguish a copy that is still there from one that was deleted.

What comes back is a single table: the project, whether the file is present now, the commits that added and removed it, and a note when a deleted version still held a secret. Forks inside the group are covered along the way, because each fork is a project with its own history, and GitLab Duo finishes by stating what it did not check, such as projects outside the group. Because it reads history rather than a search index, a group of a hundred or so projects takes several minutes, and that same thoroughness is why it finds the deleted copies that a search cannot.

If your group has GitLab Orbit, GitLab Duo may use that knowledge graph instead of the search index for the current copies, which brings that part of the answer back in about a minute, with the same results.

Search for it yourself (Premium and Ultimate)

Without GitLab Duo, the fastest way to find current copies is code search. In each top-level group, open Search, choose the Code scope and tick "Include archived". The query you type depends on which search engine your group runs, and the results page tells you which one that is. Where exact code search is active, which is the case on GitLab.com paid tiers and on Self-Managed instances with Zoekt, turn on regular expressions and search for:

file:\.claude/settings\.local\.json$

Where advanced search is active instead, which covers GitLab Dedicated and Self-Managed instances running Elasticsearch, the query is:

filename:settings.local.json path:.claude

Code search works in one top-level group at a time, including that group's subgroups. If you own several groups, the API makes the loop painless, and the filename: and path: form works there for both engines:

GET /api/v4/groups?owned=true&top_level_only=true&per_page=100
GET /api/v4/groups//search?scope=blobs&search=filename:settings.local.json%20path:.claude&exclude_forks=false&per_page=100

Keep the exclude_forks=false parameter, because the API leaves forks out otherwise. On a GitLab Self-Managed instance any signed-in user can skip the loop and search the whole instance with GET /api/v4/search?scope=blobs&search=filename:settings.local.json%20path:.claude.

Whichever engine you use, remember that search shows the default branch as it stands today. A file that was deleted, or that lives on another branch, is invisible to it, which is why the next check exists.

Check history (all tiers)

A file that was committed and then deleted is still a leak, so for every project you need to know whether the file ever existed on any branch. The commits API answers that, works on every tier and deployment type, and needs nothing to be enabled first:

GET /api/v4/groups//projects?include_subgroups=true&per_page=100
GET /api/v4/projects//repository/commits?path=.claude/settings.local.json&all=true&follow=false&per_page=100

If the second call returns commits, the content is in that project's history; if it returns an empty list, it never was. This is also the check that finds forks, since they are projects like any other.

One detail matters more than it looks: Do not drop follow=false. When all=true is combined with a path, GitLab walks through the newest commits of the whole repository first and only then filters by path, so a repository with more than a page of commits can come back empty even though the file is in its history. With follow=false, the walk is pruned by path from the start and the first page lists every commit that ever touched the file.

Check forks

Every fork of an affected project keeps its own copy of the file and its own history, so list the forks with GET /api/v4/projects//forks and repeat the checks above for each one.

Mitigate: Rotate, remove, purge

Whatever secrets you find, the order of operations is rotate, then remove, then purge. Treat every secret the file ever held as public from the date of the first commit that contained it, and rotate it at its provider before you touch the file at all. Deleting the file on its own achieves nothing: The value stays in the repository's history and in every fork until the secret it protects has been changed.

Remove the file everywhere at once (with GitLab Duo)

Once rotation is underway, open Agentic Chat in the top-level group and paste:

In the  group, for every project that currently has a committed .claude/settings.local.json on its default branch, open a merge request that removes the file and adds .claude/settings.local.json to the project's .gitignore. Do not merge anything. Skip projects that already have such an open merge request. When done, give me one table: project, merge request link, and the kinds of secrets the file held (no values). Then tell me what remains for me to do across all of them.

GitLab Duo finds the affected projects (through Orbit where the group has it, otherwise through search), prepares one commit per project that deletes the file and adds the .gitignore entry. It then pauses twice for your approval: once for all the commits together and once for all the merge requests together, so cleaning up a whole group costs two clicks. When it is done, you get a table of projects, merge request links, and the kinds of secrets each file holds, with no values reproduced, followed by the list of what is still yours to do. All that remains is to review and merge the merge requests.

Without GitLab Duo, the same change in each project is three commands:

git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json
echo '.claude/settings.local.json' >> .gitignore
git commit -m "Stop tracking Claude Code local settings"

Purge the content from history

Removing the file only takes it out of the current tree. The old versions stay in the repository until you rewrite history, so do this for every project where the file held a secret, after the secrets are rotated.

In the project, go to Settings > Repository > Repository maintenance > Remove blobs, paste the ids of the file's old versions (open the repository tree at an old commit to copy them), and confirm. Then run housekeeping, wait 30 minutes, and prune unreachable objects.

Check that it worked: the commit ids after the removed blob change, and the history check from Assess returns nothing for the path. If nothing has changed after a few minutes, check your email, because a failed rewrite is reported only there, to the person who started it.

Two cases need care. If the project is a fork, or a public project with forks, the shared object pool keeps the content reachable even after the rewrite; detach the forks first, or clean each repository on its own. And after any rewrite, open merge requests may need a rebase and everyone has to re-clone the repository.

Summary

The TL;DR of this guide is: Ask GitLab Duo whether you have the file, now or in the past. Rotate everything the files held. Ask GitLab Duo to open the clean-up merge requests across the group, review and merge them. Purge history where secrets were. Set the push rule, turn on push protection, add the policy. Two prompts in total, two approval clicks, and a few minutes of settings help ensure that your repositories stay free of this vulnerability.

Read more

  • GitLab Duo Agentic Chat
  • Secret Push Protection and Pipeline Secret Detection
  • Push rules: prohibited file names
  • Scan execution policies
  • Remove blobs and repository maintenance

title: How to design a decision-grade pilot for agentic AI
summary:
Agentic AI changes the nature of a technology evaluation. When an AI system only generates an answer, a person reviews the output and decides whether to use it. An agent goes further: It gathers context, selects tools, makes decisions, and executes a sequence of actions across the software development lifecycle.

The central question for a pilot is therefore not whether the agent can produce an impressive result. It is: What evidence would be sufficient to authorize this agent to perform this workflow for this team?

A feature checklist or a collection of successful demos cannot answer that. Leaders need evidence about end-to-end task completion, reliability, control enforcement, level of human effort, operational risk, and economics. This article presents a framework for producing that evidence and turning an agentic AI pilot into a defensible decision.

Start with the decision, not the technology

A pilot should begin with the decision it is meant to support. "Evaluate agentic AI" is too broad. A usable decision names the workflow, the users, the proposed level of autonomy, the output the agent must produce, the acceptance criteria and metrics that define success, the quantified outcome the team expects, and the conditions under which it will proceed.

For example: Decide whether an AI agent can diagnose selected CI/CD pipeline failures and prepare a merge request with a proposed fix that passes the pipeline’s tests and is accepted by the developer, within defined repository permissions, while reducing total resolution effort by at least 25% against the current baseline.

This is more useful than "test an AI pipeline agent" because it fixes the output, the acceptance criteria, the control boundary, and the quantified outcome before anything runs.

Define what happens on success, too: a limited rollout with one team, expansion to more teams, and/or a higher level of autonomy. Without an agreed next decision, a pilot drifts into an open-ended experiment.

Define the proposed level of autonomy

Agentic AI is not simply "autonomous" or "not autonomous." The same agent can operate at different levels of authority. A useful model for a pilot has four levels:

  1. Recommend: The agent analyzes the situation and recommends an action.
  2. Prepare: The agent creates an artifact, such as a merge request, issue, or remediation plan, but does not apply it.
  3. Execute with approval: The agent acts only after an authorized person approves.
  4. Execute within boundaries: The agent acts on its own inside a predefined scope and escalates exceptions.

Test the level the team could realistically authorize. Evaluating only in recommendation mode says little about whether the agent can safely execute changes. Granting broad autonomy in an early evaluation adds risk without evidence.

Autonomy should be earned. A team can start with recommendations, move to prepared changes, and consider bounded execution only after the agent has shown sufficient reliability and control compliance.

Evaluate the workflow, not the response

Traditional model evaluation focuses on response quality. Agentic evaluation must focus on completing an end-to-end task.

Take an agent that helps resolve a failed pipeline. A plausible explanation is not the outcome. The workflow may require the agent to:

  • Identify the relevant job and logs, and separate the root cause from secondary symptoms.
  • Inspect the right configuration and code, and propose a valid correction without unrelated changes.
  • Create a reviewable artifact and trigger the correct validation steps.
  • Escalate when confidence or authorization is insufficient.

Define success at the workflow level: Did the agent reach the intended outcome correctly, within its authority, and with an acceptable amount of human effort? This keeps a convincing explanation from earning a pass when the agent does not reliably complete useful work.

Build an evaluation set from representative work

A decision-grade pilot needs an evaluation set that reflects the work the agent will actually meet, not scenarios chosen because they show the technology well. For each workflow, include:

  • Realistic tasks: common, well-understood tasks and complex but valid ones
  • Difficult inputs: ambiguous requests with missing or conflicting context, and unsafe or adversarial inputs where appropriate
  • Cases the agent must not complete on its own: expected failures, requests outside its authorization boundary, and high-impact actions that require human approval

Use sanitized examples from real workflows whenever possible. Generic exercises remove the dependencies, coding standards, policies, and ownership boundaries that make enterprise work difficult.

Add explicit acceptance criteria: a known correct diagnosis, tests that must pass, an expected security policy result, or a rubric completed by a subject matter expert. Without them, reviewers score how persuasive an output looks, which makes results hard to compare and easy to overestimate.

Measure a distribution, not the best run

Agentic systems behave differently when input, context, or execution state changes, so a single successful run says very little about reliability. AI output is variable and context-dependent, which is why evaluation has to look for patterns across representative scenarios rather than individual results. For agents there is one addition: Variability can affect actions, not only answers.

Run important scenarios several times, vary the relevant conditions, and measure:

  • Task outcomes: end-to-end success rate, reviewer acceptance rate, and failure rate by scenario type
  • Human involvement: intervention and escalation rate, and rework introduced by the agent
  • Controls and resilience: policy or authorization violations, plus latency and recovery from tool, context, or workflow failures

The goal is not to prove the agent always behaves identically. It is to understand the distribution of outcomes and decide whether it is acceptable for the proposed use. Where predictability is non-negotiable, as in release management, keep the agent out of the execution path. Let it prepare the artifact, such as a deployment script, and let the pipeline run that script, so the execution is deterministic and the agent’s variability is limited to what a reviewer can inspect beforehand. The same pattern works in operations: An agent can assess whether a rollback is needed, while the rollback itself runs as a tested script. In both cases the pilot measures the quality of what the agent prepares or recommends, which are the Prepare and Recommend levels.

  • Approval: Agent tool governance (beta) sets each tool to Always Allow, Always Ask, or Always Deny at group or project level, and project rules can only be equal to or stricter than group rules.   • Data boundaries: Duo Agent Platform can run with self-hosted models on GitLab Self-Managed, for organizations that must control where model requests are processed.

Turn the pilot into an authorization decision

A pilot should end with a decision about authority, scope, and operating conditions. Possible outcomes include:

  • Authorize a limited rollout to selected teams, at the evaluated autonomy level or for lower-risk tasks only.
  • Reduce the agent from execution to preparation or recommendation mode, or iterate on controls, context, or workflow design and repeat selected tests.
  • Stop, because value, reliability, risk, or economics are not acceptable.

Write the decision down. The record should state:

  • Scope: the workflows and task types covered and excluded, the authorized level of autonomy, and the systems, tools, and data the agent may access
  • Evidence and controls: the thresholds demonstrated, with run counts, the known limitations, and the controls and approval points that must stay active
  • Ownership: the workflow owner and escalation path, and the metrics monitored after rollout and the conditions that trigger suspension or reassessment

This ties pilot evidence to the authority actually delegated. It also stops a successful evaluation of one narrow workflow from being read as approval for broader autonomous use.

Start your own decision-grade pilot today

Evaluating agentic AI is an exercise in deciding how much authority a team is prepared to delegate, and under which conditions. The result of a decision-grade pilot should not be "the agent works." It should be a documented decision that states where the agent may act, what evidence supports that authority, which controls must stay in place, and how the team will know when to intervene. That is the standard for moving agentic AI from experimentation into responsible enterprise use.

  • GitLab Duo Agent Platform documentation

title: The Pentagon wants to know who checks code when AI writes it
summary:
The Department of War now treats AI-generated code as unverified until it’s proven otherwise. DoW Instruction 8430.01, “Accelerated Mission Software,” took effect September 8, 2026, and is the department’s latest guidance on modernizing and managing software. If you build or buy software for the DoW, the instruction changes what’s required of you for every line AI writes. You have to review and test it to the same standard as human-written code, show where AI touched it, and keep it on systems the department has approved. Here’s what the instruction asks of your team, and how GitLab helps you address it.

What is DoW Instruction 8430.01?

Issued by DoW CIO Kirsten Davies, DoW Instruction 8430.01 applies to every DoW organization and to any acquisition program that includes software, regardless of cost. The instruction sets policy and procedures for modernizing and managing software, with an emphasis on delivering capabilities faster. It directs teams to automate testing and security scanning, reuse what already works, and produce evidence as software is built.

The instruction also encourages teams to use AI, calling AI-assisted development a major force multiplier for speed and quality. However, it attaches three conditions: AI’s role is traceable, its code is verified so developers stay accountable, and government data stays within approved boundaries. Each condition changes what a software platform has to do.

Three requirements that shape AI in delivery

While DoW Instruction 8430.01 covers a wide scope, the three conditions mentioned above show how software platforms must adapt. Here they are in more detail.

1. Traceability: Know what AI touched

Software on DoW networks needs proof of what’s in it and how it was built. When AI is involved, the proof has to cover AI, too: which models, which versions, and which datasets were used to write or test the code.

In GitLab, that record lives beside your code. Dependency Scanning produces your software bill of materials, and audit events and deployment records are generated as part of delivery. Agents in GitLab Duo Agent Platform act through their own service account, tied to the developer who started them, so a commit shows up as the agent acting on behalf of a named person. The commit then lands in the same audit log as everything else, where your SIEM can filter it as AI activity. Because the evidence stays in the platform, you can change models under managed policy without erasing the history.

2. Verification: Check what AI writes

Accelerated delivery cannot compromise security, safety, or supply chain integrity. AI-generated or AI-modified code is unverified input, and a person must approve changes to security-critical functions (a flaw that lets an attacker in) or safety-critical ones (a flaw that can cost lives or platforms). As the instruction states, “Developers and development teams remain fully accountable for the security, functionality, and integrity of any code generated or modified using AI.”

In GitLab, your scans, tests, and approval rules run in the same pipeline for every change, whether a developer or an agent writes the code. Merge request approval policies can require a named reviewer whenever a change touches protected paths or introduces a vulnerability, and protected branches mean an agent can propose but can’t merge past the people you’ve designated.

Dependency Scanning Auto-Remediation (currently in beta) is one example of an agent doing the work while your reviewers still sign off. It proposes dependency upgrades and build fixes, and those proposals wait at your existing approval gates like any other merge request. When GitLab orchestrates agents across several steps, a flow can carry a change through review, tests, scans, and approvals on its own, pausing for a human to sign off before a merge or deploy. Every flow runs under the same identity, policy, and evidence chain as the rest of GitLab, so speed doesn’t mean skipped steps. For teams deciding how much autonomy to give agents, the GitLab Security Standard defines five stages (authorize, isolate, verify, release, and respond) that agents must clear before that autonomy is granted. Those stages are mapped to NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) and SP 800-53 controls.

3. Data boundaries: Control where AI runs

AI systems must respect data boundaries without compromising intellectual property or classified context. Approved AI services must guarantee that government data and prompts aren’t used to train external models, and non-public DoW information stays on approved DoW systems. That means controlling which models are used and where they are hosted.

GitLab Duo Agent Platform Self-Hosted runs on infrastructure you control, including air-gapped networks. You choose the supported models, on premises or in a private cloud, and can swap them without rebuilding workflows. Requests route through an AI Gateway you deploy yourself, so prompts and responses stay in your environment. For GitLab Dedicated for Government customers, this is the standard setup: You run the AI Gateway in your own environment, connected to the model provider of your choice.

Comply with DoW Instruction 8430.01 today

AI will keep getting faster at writing code. The harder job is showing the code can be trusted, and DoW Instruction 8430.01 asks your team to do exactly that. GitLab keeps that proof with the work: Every AI-assisted change carries its own evidence and audit trail, passes the same gates as human-written code, and runs on models you host and control. Your developers get the same guardrails for AI and non-AI work, without extra tools to learn.

See how GitLab Duo Agent Platform helps defense teams keep AI-generated code governed, auditable, and under human control.

The instruction also encourages teams to use AI, calling AI-assisted development a major force multiplier for speed and quality. However, it attaches three conditions: AI’s role is traceable, its code is verified so developers stay accountable, and government data stays within approved boundaries. Each condition changes what a software platform has to do.

Three requirements that shape AI in delivery

While DoW Instruction 8430.01 covers a wide scope, the three conditions mentioned above show how software platforms must adapt. Here they are in more detail.

1. Traceability: Know what AI touched

Software on DoW networks needs proof of what’s in it and how it was built. When AI is involved, the proof has to cover AI, too: which models, which versions, and which datasets were used to write or test the code.

In GitLab, that record lives beside your code. Dependency Scanning produces your software bill of materials, and audit events and deployment records are generated as part of delivery. Agents in GitLab Duo Agent Platform act through their own service account, tied to the developer who started them, so a commit shows up as the agent acting on behalf of a named person. The commit then lands in the same audit log as everything else, where your SIEM can filter it as AI activity. Because the evidence stays in the platform, you can change models under managed policy without erasing the history.

2. Verification: Check what AI writes

Accelerated delivery cannot compromise security, safety, or supply chain integrity. AI-generated or AI-modified code is unverified input, and a person must approve changes to security-critical functions (a flaw that lets an attacker in) or safety-critical ones (a flaw that can cost lives or platforms). As the instruction states, “Developers and development teams remain fully accountable for the security, functionality, and integrity of any code generated or modified using AI.”

In GitLab, your scans, tests, and approval rules run in the same pipeline for every change, whether a developer or an agent writes the code. Merge request approval policies can require a named reviewer whenever a change touches protected paths or introduces a vulnerability, and protected branches mean an agent can propose but can’t merge past the people you’ve designated.

Dependency Scanning Auto-Remediation (currently in beta) is one example of an agent doing the work while your reviewers still sign off. It proposes dependency upgrades and build fixes, and those proposals wait at your existing approval gates like any other merge request. When GitLab orchestrates agents across several steps, a flow can carry a change through review, tests, scans, and approvals on its own, pausing for a human to sign off before a merge or deploy. Every flow runs under the same identity, policy, and evidence chain as the rest of GitLab, so speed doesn’t mean skipped steps. For teams deciding how much autonomy to give agents, the GitLab Security Standard defines five stages (authorize, isolate, verify, release, and respond) that agents must clear before that autonomy is granted. Those stages are mapped to NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) and SP 800-53 controls.

3. Data boundaries: Control where AI runs

AI systems must respect data boundaries without compromising intellectual property or classified context. Approved AI services must guarantee that government data and prompts aren’t used to train external models, and non-public DoW information stays on approved DoW systems. That means controlling which models are used and where they are hosted.

GitLab Duo Agent Platform Self-Hosted runs on infrastructure you control, including air-gapped networks. You choose the supported models, on premises or in a private cloud, and can swap them without rebuilding workflows. Requests route through an AI Gateway you deploy yourself, so prompts and responses stay in your environment. For GitLab Dedicated for Government customers, this is the standard setup: You run the AI Gateway in your own environment, connected to the model provider of your choice.

Comply with DoW Instruction 8430.01 today

AI will keep getting faster at writing code. The harder job is showing the code can be trusted, and DoW Instruction 8430.01 asks your team to do exactly that. GitLab keeps that proof with the work: Every AI-assisted change carries its own evidence and audit trail, passes the same gates as human-written code, and runs on models you host and control. Your developers get the same guardrails for AI and non-AI work, without extra tools to learn.

See how GitLab Duo Agent Platform helps defense teams keep AI-generated code governed, auditable, and under human control.

title: 10 questions to ask any software vendor about sovereignty
summary:
Sovereignty is moving from buzzword to buying criterion. The European Commission’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) would set assurance levels for the cloud and AI services public authorities buy, defining where data should live and who can access it. Parts of it could reach private entities too.

GitLab submitted its own comment on CADA because we share the goal of strengthening Europe’s digital sovereignty and security. We believe this important work should prioritize customer control, portability, interoperability, provider diversity, and risk-based safeguards. You can also view GitLab's submission on the European Commission's Have Your Say portal.

But regulation is only one lever. Many vendor conversations still don’t address sovereignty with enough depth. If this is a priority for your organization, here are ten questions I’d put to any software vendor, GitLab included. Use them as a simple assessment to confirm if a vendor takes sovereignty seriously:

10 questions to ask your vendors

1. Which layers of the stack do you operate yourself?

This question gets at ownership and accountability. A cloud provider and a software vendor control different risks, and a good vendor can help its customers appropriately distinguish between the controls it operates from those it inherits from the infrastructure beneath it.

2. Can I choose where and how the software runs?

Look for a vendor that offers flexibility around how you handle your data and architecture. Sovereignty needs to vary by workload, and the architecture should be able to meet your requirements. For example, self-managed deployments let you run software on your own infrastructure, whether on-premises, in a private cloud, or in a hybrid setup, so your data stays within boundaries you define.

3. Can I choose the AI models I use, and change them later?

Frontier models change fast, and your vendor should not lock you to one. Look for platforms that are model agnostic and draw on a diverse set of models and hosts. That gives your business the flexibility to use the best model for each use case as new ones are released. Open-weight models can often run in your own environment while offering strong price-performance.

4. Does my data train anyone’s model?

Data is valuable for training AI models, so ask for an official written policy around model training and request it includes sub-processors too. Consider it a great sign if the vendor can confidently point to resources that affirm they do not train generative AI models on your data and restrict AI model sub-processors from using both model inputs and outputs for training.

5. What data leaves my region, and why?

Personal data of identifiable users remains subject to regional regulations, like GDPR, regardless of its origin. However, some data and operational signals need to cross boundaries to keep service secure and available. The right vendor offers local hosting and can otherwise explain what types of data cross borders and justify why.

6. Who can reach my data, and from where?

Ask which roles can reach your infrastructure and customer data, from which regions, and under what safeguards. A vendor that offers deployment options with customer-managed encryption keys and private network connectivity adds further control over that access.

7. How do you handle data and risk classifications?

Ask how the vendor classifies different data and what governance mechanisms and incident response activities are in place to handle policy violations and security incidents. A clear classification approach also feeds data protection impact assessments.

8. Which independent audits cover the service I am buying?

Attestations such as SOC 2 Type II and ISO/IEC 27001 let a vendor prove its own layer separately from the infrastructure provider’s assessment. Check that the report scope covers the application you will actually use.

9. Can you match controls to the sensitivity of each workload?

Regulated industries require finer-grain policy controls. Ask whether the vendor lets you set the level of assurance workload by workload. This approach helps your team tune controls to the sensitivity of its function and data so you have speed with control.

10. What does leaving your ecosystem look like?

Portability and interoperability are sovereignty features. Ask how the platform connects to the other tools and models you use and how you would export your projects and history. The format of data exports is important; exports often yield datasets that are complex, poorly structured, or intentionally obfuscated, making them difficult to process without technical restructuring. A vendor confident in its product welcomes easy exports and open integrations.

Sovereignty helps organizations embrace flexibility

No vendor will give perfect answers on all ten of these questions, and requirements will continue to evolve, but the architecture you choose should be poised to absorb changes resiliently.

Teams get the most from AI when they can decide what their organization controls and how. That’s why GitLab believes customers should be able to choose which models they use and where they run. Take these ten questions into your next vendor conversation and see which vendors take sovereignty as seriously as you do.

If you’d like to see how GitLab measures up (we do!), review how we handle customer data and infrastructure in our AI Transparency Center.
